prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

When I was a boy and a man would die we’d say a verse when the hearse went by one car two car three car four someone knocking on the devil’s door. I smoked all night myself awake and saw the lights and the day break. When the sun was done with the final star I left the house and the door ajar and went to the church. The father was nice but the holy water was cold as ice. I found a friend and felt his hand fall through mine like crumbling sand. I went to hear the talk in the square but there were headless people there. I turned to the clock for the time of day but the hole in the wall had nothing to say. Callous of heaven and careless of hell you knew something you didn’t tell. The soul you said was only fear, and heaven, well heaven at best was here. So heaven is gone if that was it and the soul lies there in the private pit but hell is big and hell is a bone and hell comes in from the edge of alone. Hell is a dead girl who walks through the town and hunts for my bed to lay herself down.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: When, The, Callous

outputs.L1:
When I was a boy, and a man would die, we’d say a verse when the hearse went by:

One car, two car, three car, four—  
someone knocking on the devil’s door.

I smoked all night, myself awake, and saw the lights and the day break. When the sun was done with the final star, I left the house with the door ajar and went to the church. The father was kind, but the holy water was cold as ice.

I found a friend and felt his hand fall through mine like crumbling sand. I went to hear the talk in the square, but there were headless people there. I turned to the clock for the time of day, but the hole in the wall had nothing to say.

Callous of heaven and careless of hell, you knew something you did not tell. The soul, you said, was only fear; and heaven—well, heaven at best was here. So heaven is gone, if that was it, and the soul lies there in the private pit. But hell is vast, and hell is a bone, and hell comes in from the edge of alone.

Hell is a dead girl who walks through the town and hunts for my bed to lay herself down.
outputs.L2: When I was young, whenever a man died, we had a rhyme we repeated as the funeral carriage passed: first car, second car, third car, fourth—someone was rapping at the devil’s entrance. I stayed up through the whole night smoking, keeping myself from sleep, watching the lamps and then the morning arrive. After the sun had outlasted the last remaining star, I went out, leaving the house with the door partly open, and made my way to the church. The priest was kind, though the blessed water felt freezing. I reached for someone I knew, but his hand seemed to collapse through my own like dry sand falling apart. I went to the square to listen to the speech, but the people gathered there had no heads. I looked to the clock to learn the hour, yet the empty place in the wall gave no answer. You were indifferent to heaven and unconcerned with hell; you understood something and kept it hidden. You claimed the soul was nothing but fear, and that paradise, if it existed at all, was no more than this life here. If that was heaven, then heaven has vanished, and the soul remains down in its solitary grave. But hell is vast, hell is hard like bone, and hell advances from the far border of loneliness. Hell is a dead young woman moving through the town, searching for my bed so she can lie there.
outputs.L3:
The speaker begins by recalling a childhood rhyme about death, hearses, and burial. What might once have seemed like a childish or playful chant now returns with a darker meaning, shaping the atmosphere of fear and unease that follows. This memory connects the speaker’s present experience with an early awareness of mortality, suggesting that thoughts of death have always been present in the background.

After a sleepless night, the speaker leaves home at daybreak and makes their way to the church. The early morning setting creates a sense of exhaustion, isolation, and emotional heaviness. Instead of offering peace or comfort, the journey toward the church seems to deepen the speaker’s anxiety. The world around them appears bleak and unsettling, filled with signs of loss, emptiness, and disconnection.

Throughout the text, the speaker encounters images that suggest absence rather than comfort. People, places, and beliefs seem separated from one another, and the familiar structures of faith do not provide clear answers. This leads the speaker to question traditional religious ideas about the soul, heaven, and hell. Rather than accepting these ideas with certainty, the speaker examines them with doubt, fear, and confusion.

Hell, in particular, is not presented simply as a distant place of punishment after death. Instead, it becomes an overwhelming and haunting presence that seems to exist within the speaker’s own mind and experience. It is associated with loneliness, terror, and a sense of being trapped. The result is a deeply unsettling meditation on death, faith, and spiritual isolation, in which hell feels less like a doctrine and more like an inescapable emotional reality.
outputs.L4:
The text explores grief, death, and spiritual disillusionment through the voice of a first-person speaker who moves through a world that feels both familiar and dreamlike. Ordinary places—churches, streets, rooms, and gatherings—become strange under the pressure of loss. The speaker passes through community and memory as though moving through a landscape where time has come loose. The past is not safely behind them, and the dead are not fully gone. Instead, memory returns in fragments, interrupting the present and making everyday life feel haunted.

Religion appears in the text as something once meant to offer comfort, order, and explanation. The church stands as a symbol of inherited belief: a place where people gather to speak about heaven, salvation, the soul, and the meaning of death. Yet for the speaker, these ideas no longer provide peace. The rituals and promises of faith seem fragile when confronted with the reality of grief. Death is not softened by doctrine, and heaven does not appear as a clear or consoling destination. The speaker’s experience suggests that spiritual language can fail precisely when it is most needed.

As the journey continues, conventional ideas of heaven and the soul begin to collapse. The soul is not presented as something easily released from suffering, nor is heaven imagined as a simple reward beyond earthly pain. Instead, loss makes these beliefs feel distant, abstract, or even impossible. The speaker cannot escape the physical and emotional weight of absence. What remains is not certainty but disillusionment: a sense that the old explanations have broken apart, leaving behind unanswered questions and a deep loneliness.

In this vision, hell is not a fiery afterlife or a place of punishment after death. Hell is intimate, internal, and immediate. It is the loneliness that follows the speaker into ordinary life. It appears in silence, in memory, in the gap left by someone who is gone. It invades familiar spaces and transforms them, making the everyday world feel uncanny and unbearable. Hell is not elsewhere; it is here, woven into the speaker’s perception of time, community, and self.

The text ultimately presents grief as a force that unsettles every stable belief. It distorts time, estranges the speaker from others, and turns religious consolation into something uncertain. Through its surreal movement across church, community, memory, and death, the text reveals a world in which loss cannot be neatly explained or redeemed. What remains is a haunting recognition: that the deepest suffering may not lie in some distant afterlife, but in the living loneliness that grief creates.
outputs.L5:
**When The Callous**

When the world grows quiet after a difficult day, the heart often remembers what the mind tries to forget. There are moments when kindness feels rare, when people seem distant, and when the callous words of others leave marks deeper than anyone can see.

The callous person may appear strong, untouched by emotion or regret, but often that hardness is only a shield. Beneath it may be fear, disappointment, or pain left unhealed for too long. Still, cruelty should never be mistaken for strength. True strength is found in patience, empathy, and the courage to care even when life has not been gentle.

When the callous actions of others challenge our peace, we have a choice. We can become bitter, or we can choose to remain human. We can answer coldness with dignity, distance ourselves when needed, and protect the softness that makes us compassionate.

The world does not need more hardness. It needs people who understand that every word matters, every action leaves an impression, and every moment is a chance to be kinder than before.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dark, surreal prose-poem in the style of a Southern Gothic elegy, with nursery-rhyme rhythms, about grief, atheism, hell, and a dead girl haunting the speaker.
counterfactuals.output:
At the edge of the field where the kudzu prays  
with its green hands over the ruined cars,  
I buried my faith in a mason jar  
and forgot where I put it.

Hush now, hush now,  
the blackbird said,  
your little God’s gone  
under the bed.

The house leaned close to hear me breathe.  
It had the breath of rain-soaked wood,  
of hymnals molded shut in pews,  
of Sunday dresses gnawed by moths.  
All night the rafters ticked like teeth.  
All night the moon came up in rags.

And she was there—  
the dead girl, pale as buttermilk,  
barefoot in the hallway dust,  
her hair full of riverweed,  
her mouth stitched shut with water.

She rocked in the chair that had not rocked  
since my grandmother’s bones were laid  
beneath the red clay, hard as hunger.

Rock-a-bye, sinner,  
in the tree,  
down comes mercy,  
down comes me.

I told her there was no heaven.  
I told her there was no shining gate,  
no trumpet wound around the dawn,  
no Lord to lift the little drowned  
from the ditch, the crib, the feverbed.  
Only worms in their white congregations.  
Only dirt with its patient appetite.

She smiled like a cracked porcelain lamb.

Then what, she asked without asking,  
is this place?

And the house grew hot.

Not fire-hot, not furnace-hot—  
but August-in-the-blood hot,  
Bible-black and mosquito-sweet,  
the heat of a cellar where secrets swell,  
where peaches rot in jars and burst,  
where every sin your mother swallowed  
comes crawling back with your father’s eyes.

Hell, I said, is what the living make  
when the dead won’t stay put.

Hell, she said, is a nursery song  
you cannot stop remembering.

Mary, Mary,  
quite contrary,  
how does your graveyard grow?  
With wedding rings  
and angel wings  
and little girls all in a row.

She followed me through the cotton rows,  
through the chapel with its bell torn out,  
through the creek where the minnows flashed  
like scraps of broken commandments.  
She left wet footprints on the dust.  
She hummed where no throat was.  
She held my shadow by the hand.

I cursed the sky for being empty.  
I cursed the stars for looking lit.  
I cursed the moon, that old white widow,  
for wearing grief like a borrowed veil.

But nothing answered.

Nothing answers beautifully,  
if you listen long enough.

The dead girl sat at my table  
and counted my ribs with a butter knife.  
One for sorrow.  
Two for shame.  
Three for the Lord who never came.  
Four for the hole where prayer had been.  
Five for the wages of skin upon skin.

I said: child, I have no soul to save.  
She said: then why does it hurt there?

And she pointed  
not to my heart  
but to the space behind it—  
that locked room in the meat  
where a hymn was still pacing,  
thin and starved and wild.

Outside, the magnolias opened their white mouths.  
Inside, the mirror filled with swamp water.  
The dead girl climbed into my reflection  
and wore my face like a mourning bonnet.

Now when I speak, her voice comes first.  
Now when I sleep, she tucks me in  
with cold hands smelling of creek mud.  
Now when I dream, I dream of churchyards  
where no one rises,  
though the ground keeps breathing.

Hush now, hush now,  
don’t you cry.  
Ain’t no ladder  
to the sky.

Only the porch light swinging.  
Only the hound dog howling at nothing.  
Only the red clay taking all names back.  
Only the dead girl at the foot of my bed,  
bright-eyed as judgment,  
soft as a curse,

singing me down  
and down  
and down.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a Cormac McCarthy-like monologue after a death: biblical, bleak, punctuation-light, with images of a hearse, a church, headless people, a broken clock, and hell as loneliness.
counterfactuals.output:
The hearse went slow through the rain like some black ark bearing no covenant and no promise. Its lamps burned pale in the morning and the tires whispered over the road as if the earth itself had learned to hush.

At the church the doors stood open. The people gathered there in their dark coats and none of them seemed to have faces. Heads bowed so low they might as well have been headless. Hands folded. Mouths sealed. A congregation of stumps beneath the white steeple while the bell above them tolled and tolled though no man could say for whom anymore.

Inside the vestibule a clock had fallen from the wall and broken on the stones. Its hands lay crossed like bones. Time had come apart there and no one stooped to mend it. The mourners stepped around it as they stepped around all ruin. Carefully. Without witness. Without blame.

They carried him in and set him before the altar. The candles trembled. The preacher spoke of mercy but his voice was dry as dust in a cup. He spoke of the valley and the shadow and the house with many rooms. Yet all I could think was that if hell was real it was not fire. It was not chains nor teeth nor the old pit roaring beneath creation.

Hell was a room where no one answered.

Hell was the road after the hearse had passed.

Hell was the church emptied of singing and the broken clock ticking no more and all the headless sorrow of the living moving on through the rain as if to be alone were the first law written and the last.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a free-verse horror poem narrated by someone mourning a friend, mixing childhood funeral rhymes with existential dread and ending with a ghostly dead girl coming to his bed.
counterfactuals.output:
We buried you under a sky  
the color of old dishwater,  
while the grown-ups held their hats  
and lied softly into the rain.

Ashes, ashes,  
we all fall down—

I remembered us at seven,  
lining beetles in a matchbox coffin,  
singing for them in the ditch:

Here comes a candle  
to light you to bed,  
here comes a chopper  
to chop off your head.

We laughed then.  
Death was only a game  
with muddy knees,  
a dare behind the church,  
a word we could spit out  
and run from.

Now your name is a stone.

Now the worms know more  
than I do.

At night I sit with the lights on  
and feel the room expanding,  
walls pulling away  
like the universe itself  
is tired of holding anything close.

What are we,  
but little mouths in the dark  
calling to one another  
across a field of graves?

One, two, buckle my shoe.  
Three, four, shut the door.  
Five, six, pick up sticks—  
bones, maybe,  
white and patient  
under the black earth.

I keep thinking  
there must be a door somewhere  
you opened by mistake,  
a place past breath,  
past clocks,  
past mothers crying into gloves.

But the stars say nothing.

The dirt says nothing.

Even God, if He is there,  
keeps His face turned  
like a child pretending not to hear  
the counting:

Seven, eight, lay them straight.  
Nine, ten, never again.

Tonight the rain taps  
with your fingernails.

The floorboards whisper  
with your weight.

I wake before dawn  
to the smell of wet flowers  
and grave soil,  
and there she is—

the dead girl  
we used to know from school,  
pale as a nursery sheet,  
hair dripping black water,  
standing beside my bed.

She bends close.

Her lips are blue.

She says your name  
in a voice full of earth,

then climbs in beside me,  
cold as the bottom  
of the world.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: I need an original literary passage that sounds like an old folk curse or funeral chant, moving from a boyhood rhyme to a nightmare vision of heaven being gone and hell arriving.
counterfactuals.output:
When I was a little lad, I sang by the stile,  
pennies in my pocket and milk on my smile:  
“Blackbird, blackbird, hop from the thorn,  
tell me where the dead men go at morn.”

The blackbird laughed with a beak full of rain,  
“Over the hill and back again.”  
So I clapped my hands and I stamped my shoe,  
for the sky was gold and the world was new.

O hush now, child. O hold your breath.  
The rhyme has grown teeth in the mouth of death.

The stile is split and the lane is clay,  
the pennies are green and the milk is gray.  
The blackbird hangs where the church-bell swung,  
with a grave-worm curled in its little red tongue.

“Blackbird, blackbird, hop from the thorn,  
tell me where the dead men go at morn.”

No hill. No gate. No harps in the air.  
No white road rising. No angels there.  
The candles are drowned and the psalms are done,  
and the Lord’s own house has lost the sun.

Down come the stars like cinders cast,  
down comes the moon with her face nailed fast.  
The graves all knock with their knucklebone hands,  
and the sea walks over the meadowlands.

I saw heaven emptied like a beggar’s bowl,  
saw its blue roof torn and its bright bells stole;  
saw saints go wandering, blind in the snow,  
asking each crow where the blessed folk go.

Then up from the ditch and up from the well,  
red-mouthed and root-black, clambered hell.  
It came with a baby’s tune in its throat,  
it came in a widow’s weather-stained coat.

It came with a fiddle made out of bone,  
playing the names of the dead one by one.  
It came with a lantern, it came with a grin,  
and it opened the door where God had been.

So bite your thumb and bar your door,  
scatter salt on the kitchen floor.  
If you hear little feet in the nettles run,  
do not look out for your mother’s son.

For the rhyme we sang by the stile at morn  
was never for blackbird, never for thorn.  
It was a nail, and the nail was driven;  
it was the song that unstitched heaven.

“Blackbird, blackbird, hop from the thorn—”  
Hush, little ashes. Hell is born.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a grim, poetic stream-of-consciousness piece with minimal punctuation about a man walking through town after a death, encountering religious imagery, philosophical despair, and a haunting female corpse.
counterfactuals.output:
He walks because the room behind him has learned to breathe without her

and the town opens its wet black mouth

streets shining like old wounds  
windows watching with their cataract lamps  
rain threading the gutters with silver wire  
and somewhere a bell is striking the hour as if time were a body nailed up for all to see

he does not know whose death he carries  
hers  
his  
Gods perhaps  
the small death of a name no longer answered when spoken into the dark

At the church door the saints stand pale and chipped in their niches  
hands lifted in blessing or surrender  
their stone eyes worn smooth by centuries of begging  
and the Christ above the lintel hangs in the weather  
ribs like a broken cage  
head bowed not in mercy but exhaustion

Forgive them he thinks  
then cannot remember who them is  
the living perhaps  
the ones who continue  
the ones who eat breakfast beside empty chairs  
the ones who say she is in a better place because they are terrified she is nowhere at all

The candles inside gutter like souls with too little oil  
red glass cups trembling  
each flame a little tongue trying to explain suffering to the ceiling

He sits in the last pew  
where dust and shadow gather like parishioners  
and thinks of philosophers with their clean hands  
their books stacked against the abyss  
their sentences like ladders lowered into nothing  
being and nothingness  
will and representation  
the eternal return of grief in different coats

All of them wrong  
all of them right  
all of them dead

Outside the market square is empty  
the fountain mutters to itself  
a bronze angel pours black water from an urn forever  
forever being the cruelest word ever taught to stone

He passes the butcher with its hooks gleaming  
the bakery gone cold  
the apothecary window full of jars where roots float like drowned infants  
and above the rooftops the moon appears  
thin  
indifferent  
a fingernail scratching at the lid of the world

Then he sees her

not in memory  
not in dream  
not in the forgiving blur of rain

she stands at the end of the lane in her burial dress  
white ruined at the hem  
hair unbound and heavy with river water though there is no river here  
skin luminous with the patience of the grave  
mouth slightly open as if she has walked a long way to ask one question and forgotten it

His heart becomes a fist around ash

She is beautiful in the way winter is beautiful  
in the way knives are beautiful  
in the way a chapel is beautiful after everyone who prayed in it has died

He wants to run to her  
he wants to run from her  
he wants to fall down and put his face against the stones and confess to every sin he never committed simply to make the universe answer

But she only looks at him

with eyes emptied of accusation  
emptied of love  
emptied even of death  
and in that emptiness he sees the whole town reflected  
the church  
the saints  
the locked doors  
the rain  
his own face blurred and aging and absurd

He understands then that grief is not a wound

a wound has edges  
a wound knows where the body ends

grief is the town  
the rain  
the bell  
the road continuing under his feet  
grief is the dead woman standing where the street narrows  
grief is the living man unable to become stone

He whispers her name

or thinks he does

The bell answers  
or does not

The corpse raises one pale hand  
not beckoning  
not blessing  
only lifting it as if to feel whether the world is still falling

and it is

it is falling through God  
through reason  
through every bright lie ever placed like a coin upon the tongue of the dead

The town goes on shining black beneath the rain

and the man walks toward her

because there is nowhere else to go  
because every road after death leads inward  
because the grave is not beneath the earth

but waiting patiently in the human heart
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
